Shield volcanoes are what I always imagined as a kid when someone said volcanoes. They have liquid lava flows, and tend to occur out in the ocean, which brings to mind tropical pacific islands where savages made human sacrifice by throwing them into a lake of lava. The best example of a shield volcano on earth today is Mt. Kilauea in Hawaii.

Mount Kilauea is a volcano that lies directly over a hot spot in the middle of the Pacific Plate. For some reason (there are plenty of ideas why, but no one has proven it definitively) the mantle is hotter under Kilauea than the areas around it. The mantle here melts through the ocean crust (which is primarily composed of mafic rocks - this is important, particularly for my next post about strato-volcanoes), and oozes out at the surface of the ocean floor. Over a long period of time, this lava hardens into rock, and other lava flows over it, which builds up to an underwater mountain. This mountain eventually breaches the surface of the ocean, where it becomes an island. Mount Kilauea is actually taller than Mount Everest, it's just most of it lies below the surface of the ocean.

The reason shield volcanoes are called shield volcanoes is because they have a gentle slope angle, and take up a lot of real estate. For instance, the largest known mountain is an extinct shield volcano on mars called Olympus Mons. It's the tallest mountain in the solar system, and it's also the widest. The mountain is roughly the size of Arizona (it's a bit bigger, but it's close) and if you were standing on it's slope you would think it was flat ground. The mountain is three times taller than Mount Everest, but it's slope is so low that it appears flat.

Why are they like that? Well, the lava from shield volcanoes is not very viscous, so it acts more liquid than other lavas. The reason that it is less viscous is because it is more "pure". You remember how I said that the rocks on the ocean floor are primarily mafic? That means that they have less silica than continental rocks. Mafic lavas are rich in heavy metals, and form basalts and gabbros when they cool. They don't get gunked up by silicate chains and sheets like felsic lavas do. Since these lavas flow easily, they spread out over a large surface area when they reach the surface, making a wide dome shape centered around the eruption vent.
